prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- As Hayden Henshaw was being rushed to the doctor's office after becoming ill, his father heard that his son's classmates had been struck with the deadly swine flu virus like the one sweeping through Mexico. Swine flu commonly affects pigs and occasionally infects people in contact with pigs. Patrick Henshaw called his wife immediately to have Hayden checked for it. Later, they received the bad news. Hayden had become the third confirmed case of swine flu at his Texas high school. It is a virus that has killed 68 people in Mexico and infected at least eight people in the United States. Health officials arrived at the Henshaws' house Friday and drew blood from the whole family, then told them to stay inside and away from the public, Henshaw told CNN. The whole family is quarantined indefinitely, according to CNN-affiliate KABB. Henshaw said his family was shocked when they got the news about their son. "Stunned. My wife was having a panic attack," Henshaw told the affiliate. U.S. health officials have expressed concern about U.S. cases of a swine flu virus that has similar characteristics to the fatal virus in Mexico. More than 1,000 people have fallen ill in Mexico City in a short period of time, U.S. health experts said. "This situation has been developing quickly," Richard Besser, acting director of the Atlanta, Georgia-based Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), said Friday. "This is something we are worried about." Besser said all of the eight U.S. patients have recovered.  Watch for more on the U.S. cases » . New York health officials said Friday they were testing about 75 students at a school in New York City for swine flu after the students exhibited flu-like symptoms this week. A team of state health department doctors and staff went to the St. Francis Preparatory School in the borough of Queens on Thursday after the students reported cough, fever, sore throat, aches and pains. Test results are expected as early as Saturday. The new virus has genes from North American swine influenza, avian influenza, human influenza and a form of swine influenza normally found in Asia and Europe, said Nancy Cox, chief of the CDC's Influenza Division. Swine flu is caused by a virus similar to a type of flu virus that infects people every year but is a strain typically found only in pigs -- or in people who have direct contact with pigs. There have, however, been cases of person-to-person transmission of swine flu, the CDC said. CNN's David Alsup contributed to this report.

outputs.L1:
(CNN) — As Hayden Henshaw was being rushed to the doctor’s office after falling ill, his father learned that his son’s classmates had been infected with the deadly swine flu virus sweeping through Mexico. Swine flu commonly affects pigs and occasionally infects people who come into contact with them.

Patrick Henshaw immediately called his wife and asked her to have Hayden tested for the virus. The family later received the bad news: Hayden had become the third confirmed case of swine flu at his Texas high school.

The virus has killed 68 people in Mexico and infected at least eight people in the United States.

Health officials arrived at the Henshaws’ home Friday and drew blood from the entire family before instructing them to remain indoors and avoid contact with the public, Henshaw told CNN. According to CNN affiliate KABB, the entire family has been quarantined indefinitely.

Henshaw said the family was shocked by the news about their son.

“Stunned. My wife was having a panic attack,” Henshaw told the affiliate.

U.S. health officials have expressed concern about domestic cases of a swine flu virus with characteristics similar to those of the fatal virus in Mexico. More than 1,000 people in Mexico City have fallen ill within a short period, U.S. health experts said.

“This situation has been developing quickly,” Richard Besser, acting director of the Atlanta, Georgia-based Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), said Friday. “This is something we are worried about.”

Besser said all eight U.S. patients have recovered.

Watch for more on the U.S. cases »

New York health officials said Friday that they were testing approximately 75 students at a New York City school for swine flu after the students exhibited flu-like symptoms during the week.

A team of state health department doctors and staff visited St. Francis Preparatory School in the borough of Queens on Thursday after students reported cough, fever, sore throat, aches and pains. Test results are expected as early as Saturday.

The new virus contains genes from North American swine influenza, avian influenza, human influenza and a form of swine influenza typically found in Asia and Europe, according to Nancy Cox, chief of the CDC’s Influenza Division.

Swine flu is caused by a virus similar to the type of flu virus that infects people every year, but it is a strain typically found only in pigs—or in people who have direct contact with pigs. However, cases of person-to-person transmission of swine flu have occurred, the CDC said.

CNN’s David Alsup contributed to this report.
outputs.L2:
(CNN) — When Hayden Henshaw became sick and was hurried to a doctor, his father learned that other students at Hayden’s school had contracted a deadly swine flu strain resembling the one spreading across Mexico. Although the illness usually occurs in pigs, it can sometimes pass to people who have contact with infected animals.

Patrick Henshaw immediately phoned his wife and asked that Hayden be tested. The results confirmed their fears: Hayden was the third student at his Texas high school diagnosed with swine flu.

At the time, the virus had caused 68 deaths in Mexico and infected at least eight people in the United States. Henshaw told CNN that health authorities visited the family’s home Friday, collected blood samples from everyone and instructed them to remain indoors and avoid contact with the public. CNN affiliate KABB reported that the entire family had been placed under quarantine for an unspecified period.

According to Henshaw, the diagnosis left the family in disbelief. He told KABB that they were stunned and that his wife suffered a panic attack.

American health authorities said they were troubled by U.S. infections involving a swine flu virus with features similar to those of the deadly strain found in Mexico. U.S. experts reported that more than 1,000 people in Mexico City had become ill within a brief period.

Richard Besser, then acting director of the Atlanta-based Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, said Friday that events were unfolding rapidly and that officials were concerned. He added that all eight infected patients in the United States had recovered.

Meanwhile, New York health officials announced Friday that approximately 75 students at a New York City school were being screened for swine flu after developing influenza-like symptoms during the week. On Thursday, state health department physicians and other personnel visited St. Francis Preparatory School in Queens after students complained of fever, coughing, sore throats, body aches and pain. Results from the tests were expected as soon as Saturday.

Nancy Cox, head of the CDC’s Influenza Division, said the newly identified virus contained genetic material from North American swine influenza, bird flu, human influenza and a swine flu strain generally found in Europe and Asia.

The virus responsible for swine flu resembles a form of influenza that circulates among humans each year, but this particular strain is ordinarily seen only in pigs or in people who have had direct exposure to them. Nevertheless, the CDC said previous instances of human-to-human transmission had occurred.

CNN’s David Alsup contributed to the report.

Texas student Hayden Henshaw became the third confirmed case of swine flu at his high school. In response, health officials tested every member of Henshaw’s family and ordered them to remain in quarantine indefinitely as a precaution against further transmission.

The case emerged amid a growing international outbreak. In Mexico, swine flu had reportedly killed 68 people and sickened more than 1,000 people in Mexico City. At least eight infections had also been confirmed in the United States. U.S. health officials were particularly concerned because the virus found in domestic cases appeared similar to the deadly strain circulating in Mexico, although all eight American patients had recovered.

Meanwhile, health authorities in New York were investigating another possible cluster. Approximately 75 students in Queens had developed flu-like symptoms and were being tested to determine whether they had contracted swine flu.
outputs.L4:
U.S. health officials intensified their investigation into emerging cases of swine flu linked to a deadly outbreak in Mexico. Public-health workers tested students who had become ill, collected blood samples from affected families, and ordered quarantines in an effort to determine how widely the virus had spread and prevent further transmission.

Eight patients in the United States, including a high school student in Texas, had recovered from the illness. Although no U.S. deaths had been reported among those cases, officials remained concerned because the virus appeared to be spreading rapidly and had been associated with fatalities in Mexico.

The contrast between the relatively mild U.S. cases and the more severe outbreak across the border raised questions about whether the same virus was responsible, why its effects appeared to differ, and whether additional infections had gone undetected. Authorities therefore expanded testing and surveillance, especially in communities where patients had reported flu-like symptoms or possible exposure to infected people.

Health officials urged doctors, schools, and local agencies to remain alert for symptoms and to report suspected cases promptly. The investigation focused on identifying new infections, tracing contacts, and learning more about the virus’s behavior. While officials cautioned against panic, they emphasized that the combination of rapid transmission and deaths in Mexico warranted a serious and coordinated public-health response.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style breaking news report about a Texas high school student who became the third confirmed local case of swine flu during the 2009 outbreak.
counterfactuals.output:
**BREAKING NEWS**

**Texas high school student confirmed as third local swine flu case**

A Texas high school student has tested positive for swine flu, becoming the area’s third confirmed case during the growing 2009 outbreak, local health officials said.

Authorities are investigating how the student contracted the H1N1 virus and are identifying classmates, relatives and others who may have had close contact with the teenager. School officials said they are working with public health agencies and taking precautions to limit further transmission.

The student’s condition was not immediately disclosed. Officials urged parents to watch for flu symptoms, including fever, coughing, sore throat and body aches, and to keep sick children at home.

The confirmation comes as federal and state health agencies track a rising number of infections across the United States. Health officials stressed that residents should remain calm, wash their hands frequently and seek medical advice if symptoms become severe.

Further testing and additional case updates are expected.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a news article covering Hayden Henshaw’s swine flu diagnosis, his family’s quarantine, the related outbreak in Mexico, and suspected cases among students in New York City.
counterfactuals.output:
**California Boy Diagnosed With Swine Flu as Mexico Outbreak Fuels Concern**

*April 25, 2009*

Health officials are monitoring the family of 10-year-old Hayden Henshaw after the Southern California boy was diagnosed with a new strain of swine flu, amid a widening outbreak in Mexico and reports of possible infections among students in New York City.

Hayden, who lives in San Diego County, became ill with fever and other flu-like symptoms but has since recovered. His family was asked to remain at home temporarily as a precaution while public-health officials watched for signs that the virus had spread to relatives or other close contacts.

The boy had not recently visited Mexico or had known contact with pigs, raising concern that the virus was circulating from person to person. Investigators were working to determine how he became infected and whether his case was connected to other infections identified in California and Texas.

The diagnosis came as Mexican authorities closed schools and canceled public events in and around Mexico City in response to a severe respiratory outbreak. Hundreds of illnesses and dozens of deaths were under investigation, although officials had not confirmed that every suspected case or fatality was caused by the same swine-flu strain.

Concern also reached New York City, where numerous students at St. Francis Preparatory School in Queens reported fever, sore throat and other influenza-like symptoms. Health officials collected samples from several students and were testing them to determine whether they had the newly identified virus. Some students had recently traveled to Mexico, but the source of the school illnesses remained unclear.

Federal and local officials urged the public to take ordinary flu precautions, including frequent hand-washing, covering coughs and staying home when sick. They said there was no evidence that the virus could be contracted by eating properly prepared pork.

The new strain contained genetic material associated with swine, bird and human influenza viruses. Health authorities said they were investigating its severity and ability to spread while advising hospitals and doctors to report unusual clusters of respiratory illness.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a factual CNN report on early U.S. swine flu cases, including comments from Hayden Henshaw’s father, CDC acting director Richard Besser, and influenza expert Nancy Cox.
counterfactuals.output:
**CDC investigates early U.S. swine flu cases**

ATLANTA — Federal and state health officials are investigating a small number of human infections involving an unusual strain of swine influenza, including cases in Southern California and Texas.

One of the first patients identified was Hayden Henshaw, a 10-year-old San Diego County boy who developed fever and other flu-like symptoms in late March 2009. Hayden recovered without hospitalization.

His father said the illness initially appeared to be an ordinary case of the flu and that the family had not been around pigs, a detail also noted in the federal investigation.

Dr. Richard Besser, then acting director of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, said the agency was working with state and local officials to determine how widely the virus had spread. He cautioned against alarm but said the cases warranted close scrutiny because some involved human-to-human transmission.

CDC influenza expert Dr. Nancy Cox said genetic testing showed the virus contained an unusual combination of influenza genes, including components associated with swine viruses from North America and Eurasia. The pattern had not previously been identified in people or pigs, she said.

Early patients generally experienced symptoms typical of seasonal influenza, including fever, cough, sore throat and, in some cases, vomiting or diarrhea. Most recovered without serious complications.

Health officials advised people with flu-like symptoms to stay home, cover coughs and sneezes, wash their hands frequently and seek medical advice if symptoms became severe. The CDC continued laboratory testing and surveillance as investigators assessed whether the emerging strain posed a broader public-health threat.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the emerging swine flu crisis in April 2009, focusing on a quarantined Texas family, eight confirmed U.S. patients, 68 deaths in Mexico, and testing at St. Francis Preparatory School in Queens.
counterfactuals.output:
In late April 2009, health officials were confronting a possible new swine-flu outbreak spanning Mexico and the United States. A Texas family linked to suspected infection was placed under voluntary home quarantine while officials monitored symptoms and tested contacts.

At that point, the United States had confirmed eight patients—six in California and two in Texas. All had relatively mild illnesses and were recovering, with no U.S. deaths reported. Mexico, however, had reported 68 deaths associated with a severe flu outbreak, although only some had been laboratory-confirmed as the new swine-flu strain.

Concern also centered on St. Francis Preparatory School in Queens, New York, where many students became ill after some had traveled to Mexico. Samples from several students tested positive for influenza A and were sent for further testing to determine whether they had the same swine-flu virus. The episode prompted heightened surveillance and fears that the virus was spreading person to person across borders.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an urgent wire-service article explaining concerns about a new swine flu strain, its genetic origins and potential person-to-person transmission, while illustrating the story through a Texas teenager’s confirmed infection.
counterfactuals.output:
**URGENT: Novel swine flu strain raises fears of person-to-person spread**

**ATLANTA, April 24 —** U.S. health officials are investigating a new strain of swine influenza after infections were confirmed in several people, including a Texas teenager who had no known contact with pigs, raising concern that the virus may be spreading from person to person.

The teenager, one of two students in the San Antonio area confirmed to have been infected, developed a fever, cough and other flu-like symptoms before recovering. Officials temporarily closed the students’ high school as a precaution while tracing relatives, classmates and other close contacts.

The cases are troubling because genetic testing shows the virus is unlike strains commonly found in people. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said it contains a previously unseen combination of influenza genes linked to North American swine, Eurasian swine, birds and humans.

Such a mixture can emerge when different influenza viruses infect the same animal and exchange genetic material, a process known as reassortment. Pigs can harbor human, avian and swine influenza viruses, making them potential “mixing vessels” for new strains.

Investigators have not determined where the Texas teenager contracted the virus. The absence of reported exposure to pigs, together with infections among people in different locations, suggests limited person-to-person transmission may already be occurring, health authorities said.

Officials stressed that evidence of human transmission does not necessarily mean a pandemic is imminent. The central questions are how efficiently the virus spreads, whether sustained community transmission is occurring and how severe the resulting illness can be.

Symptoms have generally resembled seasonal influenza, including fever, cough, sore throat, body aches and fatigue. Authorities urged people with flu-like illness to stay home, cover coughs, wash their hands frequently and seek medical advice if symptoms become severe.

Laboratories are conducting additional sequencing and antiviral-susceptibility tests as public-health agencies expand surveillance. Officials said the investigation was moving quickly because a novel influenza virus capable of sustained human-to-human spread could pose a broader international threat.
